dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] And that's the strange part: the country that started the crash comes out on top. In 2008, the crisis started in American banks, and the dollar still rose by more than a fifth. This October, with America at war, the dollar hit its highest point in a year and a half. The fire starts in America, and the world runs into the burning house anyway, because it's still the strongest house on the street.
[serious] So America wins this crash. But the people who run the world's money are quietly betting it won't win the next one.

[serious, engaging] Last year, for the first time since 1996, the world's central banks held more of their savings in gold than in American government IOUs. And between July and September of this year alone, they bought about three hundred and twenty tons more, roughly two blue whales of pure gold.

[serious, engaging] The people who print money are buying the one thing they can't print. Because in 2022, Russia woke up to find about three hundred billion dollars of its savings frozen by the West, and every central bank asked itself: what if we're next? Every ton they buy is a bet that next time, the money runs somewhere else, to the countries piling up gold, like China.

[serious, engaging] Now, back to your answer. After 2008, someone who simply held on to an index fund was back to even within about five years, counting dividends, and the people who sold in the panic locked in their loss. The people who came through these crashes best usually had three things in common: some cash they could reach, no debt that could be called in, and the nerve not to sell at the bottom. In 1932, a lot of them weren't investors at all, just people with a skill everyone still needed, like keeping the heat and the lights working.

[serious, engaging] The last time the whole world broke, the new rules were written in a hotel in the mountains of New Hampshire. In July 1944, forty-four countries met there for three weeks and put the dollar at the center of the world, because America held about two thirds of the world's gold.
[calm, wry] Those invitations went out from Washington. The central banks buying gold right now are betting the next ones won't.
